Although neural language models (LTM) have largely displaced $n$-gram approaches due to their superior contextual understanding, we demonstrate that the robustness and speed of $n$-grams remain valuable. By integrating an $n$-gram probability distribution as a regularization term, we introduce a residual architecture for deep neural language modeling. Experiments on three standard benchmarks reveal that this method matches or exceeds the performance of state-of-the-art standalone LTMs. Furthermore, this hybrid approach enables the creation of state-of-the-art $T_3$ neural text generation models.

We examine a class of crepant resolutions of 3-dimensional algebraic varieties, specifically focusing on singularities known as non-completely intersecting cycles (ncxi), which have recently attracted significant interest. Our analysis demonstrates that the smooth varieties associated with these resolutions carry a novel, discrete set of invariants termed the graph of Laurent transformation. There exists a one-to-one correspondence linking ncxi singularities within our specified class to Laurent transformations whose support comprises totally non-negative tropical Plucker coordinates. Furthermore, we introduce a computational procedure to determine these graphs. This procedure involves identifying a specific cluster mutation pattern within an appropriately defined cluster algebra structure.

We introduce a new 3D dense facial alignment and reconstruction approach known as Self-Aligned Dual Facial Regression Networks (SADRNet). This method tackles the challenges posed by unstructured and incomplete facial images, such as missing segments or irregular boundaries, by employing a self-alignment strategy. This strategy integrates a self-aligned patch extraction module with a self-aligned generation module, both designed to function independently. Specifically, the patch extraction module identifies missing areas and generates self-aligned patches using surrounding context, while the module for generation reconstructs the entire 3D face based solely on these aligned patches. Experiments demonstrate that SADRNet surpasses current state-of-the-art methods in both dense facial alignment and reconstruction tasks.

We examine the holographic correspondence for open global symmetries, noting that while current research focuses on those admitting local cons currents, our work investigates local operators that source the explicit breaking of translational invariance. By constructing a diverse class of effective theories incorporating both localized and non-local gauge redundancies, we achieve the description of fractons associated with momentum conservation. Additionally, we identify fracton modes corresponding to the breaking of rotational symmetry. Our analysis reveals that fracton modes exhibit redundancy, a trait shared with boundary gravitons found in holographic contexts involving Anti-de Sitter (AdS) spaces with broken AdS_3/CFT_2 duality.

This investigation explores the potential generation of primordial black holes (PBHs) resulting from inflationary models within the $\alpha$-attractor framework. Our findings indicate that during the radiation-dominated era, curvature perturbations amplified on cosmological scales within this model; however, subsequent cosmic evolution causes these scales to exit the horizon again, preventing the formation of PBHs. In contrast, when considering scalar field potentials with a minimum, significant PBH generation becomes feasible if the potential slope is sufficiently steep. Furthermore, the magnitude of the generated PBHs is contingent upon the parameters of the potential and the value of $\alpha$. Specifically, for an $\alpha$ of $10^{-3}$, a PBH mass of approximately $10^{16}$ grams arises from perturbations at the cosmic microwave background (CMB) frequency, provided the potential is defined by Eq. (\ref{eq:pot}) with $\xi=100$ and the model parameters $m_{\rm p}/\sqrt{4\pi}=10^{-5}$.

Consider a labeled ordered tree with $n$ nodes, where the nodes are permuted integers from 1 to $n$. We examine $W_n$, representing the smallest value among the "root" nodes of the various $k$-level subtrees. It is important to note that these deepest roots correspond exactly to the leftmost nodes found at any specific depth. Our study establishes the probability distribution for $W_n$ and confirms that, as $n$ grows large, the scaled variable $\sqrt{2}W_n/\sqrt{n}$ adheres to an exponential distribution. Furthermore, we investigate joint moments involving the counts of tree nodes at a fixed depth $k$ that hold the minimum value within their respective level-$l$ subtrees. Our approach leverages the connection between ordered trees and plane partitions, utilizing a result by Bousmard and Saouter regarding the joint distribution of plane partition rows.

This study outlines a ballot counting system designed to deliver accurate vote tallies for elections. The proposed method integrates image processing and Optical Character Recognition (OCR) to detect and extract the selected candidate's name from a photographed ballot. This system offers a cost-effective and efficient alternative to manual counting, addressing the challenges of providing timely and reliable election results.

Existing research on time series analysis predominantly assumes that model parameters are correctly specified or that the number of parameters is finite, often neglecting scenarios involving structural misspecification where parameters are both finite but incorrectly defined. In contrast, this work investigates a setting with a linear time series model containing an infinite number of parameters, specifically examining a case of "structural misspecification" wherein the true data-generating process is captured by a finite subset of these parameters. We demonstrate that if the superfluous parameters are sufficiently uncorrelated with the remaining true coefficients, the estimator for the valid component of the parameter vector exhibits consistency, a phenomenon termed "benign misfitting." However, if these extra parameters possess strong positive correlations with the true parameters, consistency breaks down, resulting in "malicious misfitting." Additionally, we observe that benign misfitting can persist even when model selection techniques are employed to identify the correct parameters.

Speech enhancement is essential for human communication, yet speech quality is frequently compromised by environmental noise, particularly in real-world scenarios where noise is difficult to mitigate. This study introduces a complete attention bidirectional deep learning framework designed to suppress narrowband noise in single-channel speech. The model employs two gated recurrent neural networks (GRUs) arranged in a bidirectional structure to capture temporal dependencies within the spectral domain. Additionally, multi-scale complete attention mechanisms are integrated to explicitly model long-range correlations across frequencies and time. Experiments conducted on the AMI Meeting Corpus demonstrate that the proposed model achieves state-of-the-art performance, surpassing existing narrowband attention-based bidirectional deep learning methods.

Melody-based audio sharing services, such as SoundCloud and Spotify, have become widely utilized for distributing music. However, their popularity creates a vulnerability where malicious actors can exploit these platforms to disseminate harmful computer pathogens disguised as audio files. In this paper, we introduce "Virus in Tune," a novel approach that leverages existing music streaming applications to propagate malware. Our method involves injecting malicious code into the binary files of popular songs and uploading the infected tracks to a malicious server. We demonstrate that these files attract significant downloads, resulting in widespread malware infection. Our findings reveal that Virus in Tune achieves a success rate of 90% across 11 different malware families, with an average infection rate of 53.1% per melody. Furthermore, we illustrate that these stealthy propagation strategies are difficult for current anti-malware solutions to detect. Although our study focuses on music streaming, the underlying principles of Virus in Tune are applicable to other content dissemination apps, including those for videos, images, and podcasts.

This study focuses on the self-planning of a solitary, forward-looking electricity market participant who aims to maximize the profit from a specific generation unit. The objective is to determine the optimal generation schedule for a finite planning horizon, accounting for the unit's capacity limits and operational expenses. The model treats the electricity market as a Cournot game, where the participant optimizes profit by anticipating the market-clearing price and the aggregate generation of all rivals. Uniquely, this approach incorporates risk-aversion through a constraint limiting exposure to market share, which is defined as the probability that the agent's output exceeds the system's total demand. This formulation results in a complex, non-convex optimization challenge. To address this, the paper derives the first-order conditions for the Cournot strategy and proposes a tailored heuristic algorithm designed to locate the global maximum profit. Validity and performance of this method are verified through comprehensive numerical experiments.

The core objective of attosecond science is to capture and examine the dynamic evolution of electrons during fundamental chemical processes. Although various attosecond techniques have been developed to probe molecular orbitals and vibrational states, the generation of a solely electron-based method capable of generating sub-100-femtosecond coherent light remains elusive. In this study, we investigate the suitability of the K-L Auger relaxation following a core-hole creation in a potassium atom for producing coherent electron waves. Our theoretical analysis indicates that by controlling the electron wave packets emitted via the $2p \to 1s$ and $3s \to 1s$ L1,mm-to-M1,mm transitions, we can create superposition states with a period of approximately 5.4 attoseconds. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the electron charge density density associated with these states functions as an efficient tool for monitoring electron dynamics. Although the associated x-ray emission density density exhibits limited sensitivity to timing, the charge density density offers superior resolution for probing electron behavior. This finding suggests that advanced imaging modalities utilizing charge carriers could provide insights into electron dynamics with temporal resolutions surpassing those currently achievable with x-ray techniques.

These models demonstrate that as $f$ decreases, the Hadley cell expands poleward, and the magnitude of the thermal equatorial Hadley cell and associated atmospheric circulation intensifies. This study introduces fresh perspectives on the vector frequency differential formulation, specifically examining its algebraic dimensions, geometric implications, and connections to classical frequency measures. It establishes a new dimensional framework for frequency that accommodates both algebraic and geometric differential formulations, thereby revealing the fundamental dimensional components of frequency differential geometry. The paper also investigates the interplay between this proposed dimensionality and established geometric differential expressions, highlighting its relevance to the dimensional structure of frequency in differential geometry. Finally, the study presents several novel geometric differential representations of frequency, leveraging their potential to advance research in geometric frequency theory.

We present a proposal for optical phase estimation that involves creating bosonic pairs and squeezing within the circulating light of an asymmetric high-Q cavity. This cavity links two stationary electric dipole moments, which individually interact with distinct optical frequencies. We demonstrate that the phases accumulated by these dipoles serve as a resource to induce squeezing and generate a rate of duo generation in the cavity light sufficient to support efficient dual-phase detection using standard quantum limits. We suggest this approach could be scaled to form an interferometric sensor capable of measuring the phases of electric dipoles in a photonic system, thereby offering a method to observe and utilize the inherent decoherence of matter.

Phosphorus atoms in silicon serve as highly promising candidates for the n-type dopant in next-generation technologies, owing to their ability to diffuse slowly and form stable donor-impurity pairs that enable precise control over electronic states. This paper employs a full configuration interaction simulation, incorporating the complete 3C-Si band structure and the specific wave functions of P in Si, to detail the origins of the splitting observed within the $^{31}\text{P}$ nuclear spin magnetic doublet. Our findings indicate that the splitting magnitude is governed by the perturbation of valley-orbit states via the nuclear electric quadrupole moment, a phenomenon arising from the non-quadrupolar component of the electric field gradient generated by a paired V-center (donor) spin. Consequently, pairing two P atoms in silicon results in a complex spectrum characterized by multiple components, which can be decoded using this theoretical framework. Ultimately, these insights offer a pathway to fully understand and exploit spin-dependent interactions for advanced quantum logic operations within silicon-based quantum computers.

We examine the electronic transport properties of quantum trenches formed in HgTe crystals, utilizing finite-temperature non-equilibrium Green's function methods. Our findings indicate that while a four-component four-band model predicts a four-component Dirac state at the trench core, this state is typically rendered inhomogeneous and confined by geometric constraints or impurities. Consequently, a gapless quantum trench cannot be achieved when relying solely on such model-based design. We further demonstrate that a two-component Dirac state can be achieved at the trench center by introducing a specific structural asymmetry into the HgTe quantum trench.

This study evaluates a cooperative Collaborative Non-Orthogonal Multiple Access (C-NOMA) protocol involving vehicular users, where a cooperative driver assists a cooperative one in transmitting data. The performance metrics examined include the Collaborative Transmission Rate (CTR), the probability of collaborative transmission failure, and the average transmission delay. The work also assesses how system behavior evolves as the cooperation threshold varies. The analysis offers valuable insights for the advancement of cooperative autonomous driving systems.

Dynamic Time Division Duplexing (D-TDD) is a vital technology for fifth-generation (5G) mobile networks, enabling the flexible and efficient allocation of uplink and downlink transmission time slots. This study introduces a game-theoretic model for optimizing the allocation of time division duplexing in 5G networks, incorporating the specific constraints of each base station. In this framework, the time slots for the uplink and downlink are treated as continuous variables within a continuous game, where the utility function for each base station is defined by its data transmission rate. By deriving the best response function for every participant, the research characterizes the resulting data transmission rate utility as a concave function and confirms the existence of a Nash equilibrium. Furthermore, a decentralized algorithm is proposed to locate this Nash equilibrium. Analytical and simulation results demonstrate that this approach is effective, efficient, and delivers performance comparable to a centralized solution.

Neural Ordinary Differential Equation (Neural ODE) is a deep learning framework designed to solve ordinary differential equations (ODEs) by a method that learns both the function and its gradient simultaneously. This dual-learning capability, known as adjoint method, allows it to be memory-efficient, making it suitable for large-scale problems. This study introduces a novel approach, called Gradient Acquisition (GAIN), which enables the direct learning of first-order gradients within the architecture of a black-box model, without relying on the traditional adjoint technique. GAIN introduces a new constraint term into the loss function to enforce the relationship between state changes and function outputs, effectively forcing the network to learn gradients intrinsically. We successfully integrated GAIN with the state-based architecture of a Hamiltonian Neural Network (HNN), creating a unified solver that combines HNN's conservation of energy properties with the direct gradient learning capabilities provided by GAIN. Experimental results indicate that this enhanced model outperforms existing Neural ODE implementations in terms of accuracy, convergence speed, and memory utilization.

We propose a novel multi-agent system that integrates human feedback to improve trustworthiness and confidence in machine learning models. In our approach, a primary agent manages a task-specific knowledge network comprising specialized human operator agents. When incoming data streams are processed, a trusted operator identifies and corrects inaccuracies, thereby enriching the dataset. This augmented data is subsequently used to train a predictive model. Crucially, our system continuously monitors the live model's performance, automatically adjusting hyperparameters to optimize outcomes. We evaluated this human-in-the-loop multi-agent methodology against a standard baseline, demonstrating significant enhancements in overall model reliability.

Deep learning has become the leading approach for detecting prohibited items in security x-ray scanners, yet existing research relies on inadequate benchmarks that hinder practical progress. The primary flaws of current datasets include insufficient diversity in training samples and a lack of real-world relevance. To address these issues, we introduce the first comprehensive security x-ray examination benchmark, featuring ten curated datasets that offer diverse object categories, varied bag styles, and realistic operational conditions. Additionally, we propose a Lateral Suppression Module (LSM) designed to enhance detection accuracy by differentiating objects from background noise and eliminating redundant activations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed model significantly surpasses state-of-the-art results on all benchmark datasets, with particular superiority over existing leaderboards.

By selecting a specific chain $J$ and applying the $5/3$ power scaling factor to all 6j symbols in the invariant's definition, $T(J; T^2_N)$ grows exponentially proportional to the Riemann energy $E_R$. This behavior mirrors the volume hypothesis seen in LMT theory. Furthermore, under an additional constraint on $N$, the invariant exhibits sensitivity to modifications in the local connectivity between tori.

Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) stands as a significant challenge in Natural Language Processing, tasked with identifying the appropriate meaning for each word within a specific textual environment. This study introduces a method to elevate WSD performance by integrating the "context-gloss" concept. This approach leverages the "context-gloss" of word senses to enrich the contexts surrounding synonymy clusters, thereby strengthening the semantic analysis of surrounding text. Furthermore, this study presents a new "context-gloss" definition and corresponding algorithm. Empirical tests utilizing this method for WSD demonstrate its effectiveness.

We present a methodology for identifying evidence of top quark production within proton-nucleus collisions, leveraging the enhancement of gluon density and effective saturation of the proton wavefunction in the nucleus via nonlinear gluon fusion mechanisms. A comprehensive Monte Carlo simulation was employed to analyze the kinematic distributions of the resulting jets and b-jets, incorporating the effects of non-linear dynamics, parton showering, hadronization, and detector response. The analysis reveals that the distribution of b-jet transverse momentum ($p_T$) exhibits a characteristic peak, serving as a distinctive signature of the top quark generation. This signature is shown to be largely resilient against variations in the specific hadronization models utilized.

Cross-domain text-to-SQL generation entails converting natural language queries into database SQL statements, a task that demands a deep comprehension of both linguistic semantics and database schemas. A primary challenge lies in the intricate mapping between these two domains, often resulting in erroneous SQL outputs due to flawed parsing of the schema or query structure. To address these issues, we introduce a novel end-to-end cross-domain text-to-SQL framework called MCSTP (Multi-Choice Supportive Task Prediction). MCSTP decomposes complex structural reasoning into two streamlined sub-tasks: Multi-Choice Schema Link Prediction and Structural Task Prediction. By guiding the model to first identify relevant schema elements and subsequently their structural roles, MCSTP facilitates more efficient learning of structural knowledge. Experiments conducted on the Spider dataset demonstrate that MCSTP achieves state-of-the-art performance, surpassing previous leading methods by a 0.9 point improvement in Executable Accuracy.

Privacy-preserving mechanisms for data analysis are essential to enable the use of sensitive information while safeguarding individual anonymity. A significant portion of this private data, including genomic sequences, social network interactions, and mobile location histories, utilizes graphs for organization. Consequently, a substantial number of existing privacy frameworks address leakage through graph-based structures. Nevertheless, the current landscape of such frameworks remains opaque, particularly regarding their theoretical underpinnings. This work provides a thorough examination of privacy frameworks grounded on **differential confidentiality**, providing a clarification of the concepts often overlooked or insufficiently explained in prior research. We specifically analyze the realms of graph publishing, graph querying, and graph matching. For each domain, we delineate the state-of-the-art solutions, categorizing them by underlying design principles, and offer a comparative assessment of these methods. Additionally, we identify unresolved challenges and propose innovative ideas for future graph-based privacy-preserving systems, culminating in a provision of differential confidentiality-based solutions for the identified gaps.

The release of the Euclid mission's data and catalog has triggered a surge of analysis proposals, with a wide array of works already in progress or under review. This work presents a strategic framework designed to maximize the scientific value of Euclid through collaborative efforts. We outline specific proposals for joint analyses, emphasizing their collective significance. This collaborative strategy is intended to secure a prominent legacy for the Euclid mission by ensuring key scientific objectives are met through robust, unified research.

This study introduces a novel methodology for the automatic generation of challenging road networks designed to evaluate Advanced Driver Assistance Systems (ADAS) and other driver automation technologies. The proposed approach combines an evolutionary algorithm with a specialized creation operator based on Bezier curves to generate sequences of driving actions. These action sequences are executed within a driving simulator, with the resulting difficulty assessment serving as the optimization criterion. The utility of this approach is demonstrated through its application to the evaluation of an Automatic Emergency Steering system (AEAS), with results indicating that the method successfully identifies complex driving scenarios that effectively test the system's capabilities.

Describing audio content with natural language is a core capability of modern human and machine listeners, yet generating textual descriptions specifically for music playlists remains unexplored. To address this, we introduce MeloList, a large-scale dataset comprising 250,000 public music playlist descriptions, where each description aggregates the 10 track titles from popular services like Spotify. We describe our collection methodology and analyze the statistical properties and textual features of the dataset. Furthermore, we outline a new evaluation protocol for MeloList, incorporating both automatic scoring and human judgments, and present initial results from baseline models to establish a foundation for future research.

Activity detection serves as a fundamental task within video analysis, facilitating broader applications like video search and surveillance. Although numerous approaches have been proposed, the inherent complexity of human activities and the difficulty of automatically learning robust temporal patterns remain significant challenges. In response, we introduce a novel method termed Dual Context Aggregation Network (DCAN). This framework enhances the temporal discriminability of activity classifiers by consolidating two distinct contextual sources: the global video context and the specific temporal neighborhood surrounding each clip. We achieve this through dedicated global pooling and adaptive neighbor aggregation mechanisms. Experimental results on the standard ActivityNet-1.3 benchmark demonstrate that DCAN surpasses the state-of-the-art, achieving a mean Average Precision (mAP) of 41.1%.

This study investigates the emergence and fundamental nature of the I-mode observed in the JET tokamak, characterized by distinct palm tree modes. These modes manifest as localized regions of elevated electron temperature and enhanced H-alpha emission, appearing intermittently across the plasma's poloidal cross-section. Their presence correlates with a marked reduction in the volume occupied by edge-localized modes (ELMs) and a concurrent increase in the volume exhibiting high electron temperature and strong H-alpha emission. Their occurrence is linked to specific conditions within the edge transport barrier, notably a localized minimum in the local poloidal shear of the toroidal plasma current, which serves as a necessary prerequisite for their development. These phenomena are likely driven by a spontaneous reorganization of the edge turbulence spectrum, wherein the characteristic turbulent eddy size aligns with the distance to the nearest minimum in local poloidal current shear. This realignment facilitates a transition from a regime dominated by large-scale, long-pulse edge disruptions to one featuring smaller-scale, shorter-duration fluctuations. Consequently, a substantial fraction of the total fluctuation energy becomes spatially confined to the vicinity of the stability minimum, resulting in the localized hot spots that define the palm tree modes.

This study introduces a novel approach to collision prevention in mobile robots through the use of Virtual Force Fields (VFFs). The proposed method collaboratively merges individual VFFs to form shared Collision Risk Regions (CRRs), which function as dynamic, obstacle-dependent VFFs generated via linear interpolation. By applying this technique within holonomic robots, it enables the creation of diverse, adaptable, and smooth trajectories. Tested on a KUKA LBR iiLiLi robotic arm, the method demonstrates its capacity for effective collision avoidance while ensuring compliance with constraints regarding obstacle avoidance and terminal states.

This study investigates sequences of random variables $X_n$ whose probability distributions are defined by letters drawn from a finite sequence $A_n = (a(k))_{k \ge 1}$ of non-empty sets. The letter $a(n)$ is selected uniformly and independently from the $n$-th set $A_n$. Under conditions ensuring that the cardinalities of $A_n$ grow sufficiently rapidly, the paper establishes a large-scale St. Petersburg principle and develops a large-scale deviation framework. These results are then applied to demonstrate extensive divergence behaviors for various sequences $X_n$.

Current radar systems face significant challenges in hostile environments due to adversarial interference, such as noise and jamming signals. While traditional methods like spatial diversity struggle to mitigate these issues effectively, this paper proposes a new solution utilizing Intelligent Reflecting Surfaces (IRS) to enhance radar robustness. The core concept involves deploying an IRS in front of the radar to create a virtual array, which captures the target's reflections from multiple distinct paths. This approach allows the radar to estimate parameters despite the presence of jamming noise. The study specifically examines two scenarios: one where the jammer is unaware of the radar's configuration (uninformed) and another where the jammer has knowledge of the radar setup (informed). For both cases, the work derives the optimal placement for IRS elements to minimize estimation error, addressing both noiseless and noisy channel conditions. Analytical results demonstrate that the proposed method successfully suppresses jamming interference, with performance improvements being particularly pronounced against uninformed jammers. Additionally, the proposed solution for handling informed jammers yields a closed-form optimization algorithm, offering a more efficient alternative to existing heuristic approaches.

Fuzzing serves as a critical technique for uncovering security flaws in software, yet the efficacy of one fuzzer over another remains difficult to gauge. This study introduces a methodology for evaluating and contrasting fuzzing strategies by analyzing the structural characteristics of the input data they generate. By extracting statistical features from inputs and employing machine learning models, we automatically classify control flow anomalies, enabling us to link specific fault-triggering input patterns to the fuzzers capable of producing them. Our analysis reveals that leading fuzzers create distinct input distributions, and our proposed framework offers practical recommendations for selecting the optimal fuzzer for a given target. Furthermore, the system identifies which types of faults a particular fuzzer can expose, allowing for the customization of anomaly detection systems to better suit fuzz-testing environments.

Pretrained models have become the standard for solving numerous deep learning tasks, yet existing evaluation datasets often contain inherent flaws that undermine their reliability. These issues include data leakage, label inconsistencies, and overfitting to specific testing samples, which can lead to misleading performance metrics. To address these concerns, we introduce OL-BB, a minimalistic benchmark designed to assess the robustness of pretrained applications in ongoing (continual) learning scenarios. By incorporating a straightforward two-stage training protocol, OL-BB effectively identifies common pitfalls such as overfitting, data contamination, and noisy annotations. We conducted comprehensive experiments on leading state-of-the-art architectures across seven established public datasets. The results reveal that most current models suffer from severe overfitting and fail to generalize to unseen clean data. Furthermore, we observed that OL-Benchmark is sensitive to hyperparameter configurations, a factor that significantly influences performance outcomes. Finally, we propose OL-Data Leakage, a novel dataset designed specifically for evaluating data leakage issues, and demonstrate its efficacy through extensive testing.

Let $(X,d)$ be a complete metric space, and $\gamma \colon [0,1] \to X$ be a continuous path. A surface $\Sigma \colon S^1 \to (X,d)$ is defined as a surface of minimal area in the metric environment $(X,d)$ relative to $\gamma$ if the diameter of $\Sigma$ under the given path $\gamma$ is minimal among all possible surfaces. We demonstrate the existence of such minimal surfaces of minimal area in $(X,d)$ relative to $\gamma$ for any given path $\gamma$, provided that the homotopy group $\pi_1(X)$ is non-trivial and the action of fundamental group on homotopy classes is non-trivial. This result generalizes previous findings by D. C. B. and others, showing that surfaces of minimal area in $(X,d)$ relative to $\gamma$ exist whenever the homotopy group $\pi_1(X)$ is non-trivial and the action of fundamental group on homotopy classes is non-trivial.

This is the third part of a trilogy investigating the long-term evolution of solutions to the Korteweg-de Viegas (KdV) equation on the real half-line, $x \in [0, \infty)$, where the asymptotic behavior at $x = +\infty$ remains constant. In this specific installment, we examine the scenario in which the limit at infinity is spatially unstable, with the asymptotic values shifting either monotonically or via a step function. We demonstrate that, provided the initial data decays sufficiently rapidly, the long-term asymptotic profile separates into distinct components: the standard asymptotic solitary waves described in earlier works, and a secondary, rapidly decaying asymptotic structure. This secondary structure mirrors the time-independent limit solutions of the Korteweg-de Viegas equation, which are characterized by rapid decay at negative infinity and a fixed, unyielding asymptotic value at positive infinity.

The formation of shape coexistence in form is a phenomenon where nuclei exhibit multiple equilibrium configurations characterized by distinct deformations and excitation energies. A key aspect of this phenomenon is the variation in the intrinsic quadrupole moment, which can be modeled using a two-level approach. This study investigates the origin of shape coexistence at non-zero spins within $^{64}$Ni, focusing on states with spin/parity $2^+$ and $4^+$ in the $2$-h, $4$-h, and mixed configurations. The analysis reveals that the competition between the energy of the high-spin states and the mixing between configurations is driven by the monopole tensor interaction. This interaction creates a balance that favors the coexistence of different nuclear shapes even at zero spin.

This study examines the computational difficulty of approximating a $\lambda$-approximate Nash equilibrium within a Lipschitz game to within an additive error of $\epsilon$. The work establishes a lower bound on the minimum information required to achieve this approximation, demonstrating that any algorithm necessitates a query count exceeding $2\Omega(\lambda^{-1}\epsilon^{-1}\log(\lambda^{-1}\epsilon^{-1}))$. The proof strategy relies on a reduction from the weighted directed graph connectivity problem. The authors further propose an algorithm that achieves the target approximation using a query count bounded by $O(\lambda^{-1}\epsilon^{-1}\log(\lambda^{-1}\epsilon^{-1}))$, thereby tightly bounding the minimum necessary queries. The analysis assumes access to a full payoff oracle, permitting unrestricted utilization of information retrieved from the game.

This study introduces a modification to standard J-fold cross-validation known as "jeered" cross-validation, which involves intentionally introducing a deliberate variance into data splits. We evaluate this technique across three NLP tasks: sentiment classification, question answering, and spam detection. The findings indicate that jeered cross-validation yields more reliable and consistent estimations of a model's true performance compared to conventional cross-validation methods.

Absorption spectroscopy in alkalogene (Sr) elements at telecommunication wavelengths is recognized as a leading candidate for next-generation optical clocks. A key factor in its widespread adoption is the ability to accurately model and account for photon recoil effects, which significantly influence the spectral line shape. This study presents a comprehensive theoretical framework describing recoil phenomena in single-beam absorption spectroscopy, specifically analyzing the combined dynamics of photon absorption and subsequent spontaneous emission within an ultracold strontium vapor. The developed theory is then utilized to interpret experimental data from a Sr furnace, demonstrating that including recoil calculations is essential for achieving the high measurement accuracy required for optical clock applications.

Using the $\mathbf{J}_\textbf{1}$-$\mathbf{J}_\mathbf{1}$ model, which describes two honeycomb layers separated by weak interlayer couplings, we investigate twisted fluid and superfluid states of triplons. While the role of search engines in shaping public knowledge is well-documented, the specific quantity of information users overlook remains largely theoretical. This study provides empirical evidence that a significant amount of relevant content is missed when relying on Google Web Search, demonstrating that personalization features such as "I'm Feeling Lucky" and the "All Answers" box result in the omission of approximately 20% of relevant information. This document introduces the initial findings from a study investigating the feasibility of a 100-GeV muon-ion accelerator, intended to serve as a foundational element for future multi-TeV machines. Achieving such high energies with muons is particularly challenging due to their tendency for rapid decay and significant emittance growth caused by phase mixing and ionization. In contrast, protons and other stable ions offer a more viable path, provided that space charge effects are managed effectively. This research demonstrates that a 100-GeV muon-ion beam can be realized by integrating a high-intensity, high-emittance linac stage with a high-efficiency recirculating ring system.

This study introduces a motion-corrected, free-breathing 4D T2-weighted turbo spin-echo (TSE) sequence designed for whole-body imaging that accounts for respiration. The sequence dynamically adjusts slice thickness and inter-slice gaps in real time to match organ motion, thereby preventing signal gaps and artifacts like aliasing caused by gaps between slices. A retrospective analysis examined 10 patients scanned without holding their breath, using a respiratory sensor to track movement. The acquired raw data were reconstructed into a 4D dataset comprising a breathing curve and multiple 3D volumes corresponding to specific respiratory phases. These 3D volumes were generated via interpolation at thickness levels adjusted for motion, while respiration curves were derived from the 4D sequence. The resulting motion-adjusted 3D datasets were compared against those created from a respiratory-triggered, breath-hold sequence. Image quality was evaluated across five organ groups: head, chest, abdomen, pelvis, and extremities. The study found that motion-corrected free-breathing 3D datasets produced image quality comparable to both breath-hold 3D sequences and conventional 2D sequences. Additionally, the motion-adjusted 3D sequences successfully captured both shallow and deep breathing states, whereas the free-breathing 2D sequences were limited to shallow respiration. This paper addresses control synthesis for secure control in nonlinear systems subject to both safety and liveness constraints. A specific Input-Limited Control Barrier Function (IL-CBF) is introduced to enforce safety by restricting state trajectories within a designated safe set via controlled entry and exit velocities. The proposed approach guarantees safety through a combination of state-feedback control and input limitations. Furthermore, the control synthesis method ensures liveness by synthesizing a supervisor that manages the application of state-feedback control. The proposed controller is demonstrated on an autonomous vehicle navigating an intersection while adhering to safety and traffic rules.

Test metrics are essential for evaluating software development efficiency, yet creating effective tests remains a challenging task. Our findings demonstrate that SEP efficiently filters out redundant test cases, retaining only those with significant value.

Graph neural networks (GNNs) have emerged as a dominant approach for addressing node-level and graph-level tasks across various domains, such as drug discovery, social media analysis, and financial forecasting. Despite their success, GNNs frequently suffer from "over-smoothing," a phenomenon where nodes within highly connected components yield nearly identical predictions, leading to significant performance degradation. Addressing this issue is critical for maintaining reliable and robust models. In this paper, we introduce GraphPruner, an approach designed to enhance GNNs by automatically identifying and isolating densely connected subgraphs that contribute to over-smoothing. We evaluate GraphPruner on five datasets, demonstrating that it effectively mitigates over-smoothing, improves predictive accuracy, and maintains training efficiency. Additionally, GraphPruner significantly improves model interpretability by highlighting the specific subgraphs responsible for performance issues.

Adaptive random projection methods, such as CountSketch, are essential tools for estimating high-dimensional vectors from sparse data. The article establishes that these adaptive data structures maintain strong guarantees for several critical algorithms, including the Hamming distance estimator, the $\top_k$-approximate closest pair finder, and the top-$\ell$-dimensional sparse subspace embeddings.

This article examines gravity's classical Lagrangians, beginning with the linearized gravitational field around Minkowski space and a minimal coupling electromagnetic interaction. It subsequently analyzes the derivation of the Einstein-Hilbert Lagrangian density via the Palatini formalism, which treats the metric and affine connection as independent variables. Finally, the paper explores the equivalence between this standard approach and the first-order formalism, often referred to as the "Bergmann-Compton Lagrangian," that reformulates the theory using the linearized field with an incorporated minimal coupling to electromagnetism.

We examine high-energy scattering between two energy density slabs within a dual conformal field theory, utilizing the gravitational approximation in the associated large-$N$ dual string theory. This analysis focuses on regimes where slabs are extremely thin, allowing the interaction to be expressed as a power series expanding on the gradual transverse variations of the slabs. This approach addresses the breakdown of standard localized shockwave methods, which fail when slabs are not infinitesimally thin. Our findings reveal that localized shockwave approximations yield a reliable first-order estimate for the series; however, incorporating the initial correction term substantially alters the resulting geometry of the shock collision.

We examine the disparity in drag forces acting on circular objects moving through a granular medium containing fluid at rest. Specifically, we analyze horizontal translation of prisms and circular cylinders with vertical long axes, finding that drag force magnitude depends on the object's shape. Our results indicate that shape influences drag by modifying hydrodynamic flow patterns around the object, whereas scaling effects related to size do not. Additionally, shape-dependent drag is observed exclusively when hydrodynamic forces dominate over gravitational forces acting on the granular material.

The interplay between star formation and outflows remains a critical yet enigmatic area of research, with the specific mechanisms by which outflows regulate star formation still largely unknown. This study utilizes data from the DUal View (DUV) project to present spatially resolved observations of the star-forming disk in NGC 4525, a massive galaxy undergoing significant starburst activity accompanied by a prominent outflow. The findings indicate that the outflow's impact on star formation varies across different regions of the disk. Specifically, the outflow suppresses the star formation rate (SFR) surface density in the disk's center, causing it to be lower than predicted by standard models. Conversely, in the outer disk, the outflow stimulates enhanced star formation relative to model expectations. These observations support the hypothesis that outflow-induced gas compression triggers star formation in the disk's periphery, while the suppression in the center is consistent with the removal of cold gas via the outflow. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that a single global outflow parameter cannot adequately model the complex, region-dependent effects of outflows on star formation within a galactic disk.

It also defines the corresponding organizational architecture for the inference algorithms used to estimate parameter values. Collectively, BoGraph represents a novel contribution to Bayesian inference, and its efficacy is demonstrated through a case study of a costly system where data acquisition is limited, validating the approach's advantages over standard methods.

Open knowledge graphs (OKGs) have gained significant traction in recent years, serving as the foundation for numerous real-world applications. Constructing an OKG typically involves aggregating data from multiple RDF datasets, a process that necessitates a thorough pre-processing phase. A key aspect of this stage is assessing data quality, yet existing solutions are ill-suited for this task because they either lack support for distributed environments or fail to address the specific characteristics of RDF. To bridge this gap, we introduce QEREL, a novel quality evaluation structure designed with Apache Spark. Capable of running on big RDF datasets, QEREL delivers a broad array of quality metrics and is implemented as a Spark extension offering straightforward integration. The practical viability and efficacy of QEREL have been validated through a proof-of-concept study using DBpedia and Wikidata.

We introduce a novel, effective methodology for evaluating parameters in discretely monitored models, addressing the inherent challenge of high dimensionality in the likelihood function. Our approach integrates stochastic Taylor expansions with a Metropolis-Hastings Markov Chain Monte Carlo algorithm to generate an approximate posterior distribution. We validate the efficacy of this method through various simulation studies.

We present the results of a diagnostic diagram analysis for the optical spectra of the nuclei in 11 Seyfert 1 galaxies, focusing on identifying regions influenced by shocks. Our findings indicate that the majority of these active galactic cores exhibit spectra consistent with shocks, a conclusion supported by the presence of elevated [S II]$\lambda$6716/6716$\lambda$ ratios and the detection of broad emission lines with velocities exceeding 1000 km s$^{-1}$. Furthermore, we observe that the full range of shock diagnostics aligns with radiative shocks, specifically the Vishniac & Goldreich (1986) model. The data suggests these shocks occur at post-shock densities of approximately $10^5$ cm$^{-3}$ and temperatures around $1.5 \times 10^5$ K. We hypothesize that these shocks are generated by outflows originating from the central supermassive black hole, which are constrained by the AGN's ionization axis. This constraint is consistent with the observation that the velocities of the detected shocks are significantly lower than those of the narrowest lines associated with AGN photoionization.

This study introduces Event-Focused Testing (EFT), a methodology designed to generate test cases for edge applications. It leverages the generative capabilities of large language models (LLMs) combined with a purpose-built testing framework. Within our framework, an LTT is guided using three primary factors: the target function under examination, the specific event triggering that function, and preliminary test data. This guidance ensures that generated inputs produce the intended functional behavior while simultaneously triggering the associated event. We evaluated EFT against three established black-box testing frameworks across five distinct functions spanning various domains. The results demonstrate that EFT achieves a higher proportion of executions matching the desired behavior and successfully induces the target events for each function, with these advantages being particularly evident in cloud functions.

The ATLAS collaboration at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) possesses the capability to perform precision measurements regarding CP violation and rare decay processes involving beauty mesons. This paper outlines the analysis of mixing-induced CP violation in the $\Bs$ system, denoted as sin($\Phi_{\text{s}}$), as well as rare charmless decays for both B and D mesons. The analysis further explores direct CP violation in charm mesons, represented by epsilonpsilon prime over epsilon, and discusses prospects for measuring CP-violating phases within charm sector penguin box diagrams, symbolized by theta V, alongside the determination of CKM angle gamma through charm three-body charmless transitions.

Autonomous driving demands robust simulation systems capable of generating diverse and realistic driving scenarios for comprehensive algorithmic testing. However, current approaches often fall short in replicating the complex interplay between traffic rules and the varying preferences of other road users. To address this, we introduce SceneGen, a novel framework that learns scenario generation through the reinforcement learning paradigm. SceneGen utilizes a simplified traffic agent model, trained via an identical policy approach, to replicate the driving behaviors observed in actual video footage. Furthermore, by incorporating a dynamic difficulty adjustment mechanism, SceneGen ensures continuous challenges and promotes the discovery of diverse driving strategies. Extensive assessments using the nuScenes dataset demonstrate that SceneGen surpasses previous methods in recreating both the visual fidelity and statistical distributions of real-world traffic scenes. Finally, we provide an interactive platform allowing researchers to explore these generated scenes and test their algorithms within synthesized environments.

We examine the Ising model within a Cayley tree context, discovering novel weakly periodic Gibbs distributions. These distributions are characterized using a specific polynomial associated with the Cayley tree, and a linked connection to critical phenomena in the classical Ising model on such structures is also identified.

This study introduces a preconditioned iterative solver tailored for a novel class of finite difference schemes designed to approximate solutions to partial differential equations. These schemes employ a variable step size and a high-order, shape-preserving discretization known as the Shu-Dunbar scheme, which requires solving a system of nonlinear equations at each time step. While direct solvers are typically used for this purpose, they constrain the simulation's time step due to their high computational cost. To address this, the authors propose employing a Krylov subspace method to accelerate solving the associated algebraic systems. The paper derives the corresponding numerical scheme for first- and second-order linear partial differential equations with variable coefficients and demonstrates its application to a nonlinear scalar conservation law with a nonlinear flux function. Numerical results confirm that this approach enables the generation of large time steps without a corresponding reduction in temporal accuracy.

We investigate the formation of dust particles and the subsequent evolution of low-metallicity supernovae within molecular clouds. Our study focuses on two specific metal deficiency scenarios: a carbon-to-oxygen (C/O) ratio of 0.5 paired with a total metal abundance of 10% solar levels ($Z=0.1Z_{\odot}$), and an iron-depleted environment at $Z=0.02Z_{\odot}$ where iron constitutes only 10% of its typical solar proportion. This code was used to simulate the life cycles of 1 $M_{\odot}$ and 8 $M_{\odot}$ stars, specifically analyzing the impact of dust on their evolutionary trajectories and the resulting characteristics of their supernovae. Our simulations indicate that dust formation is feasible in these low-metal content clouds, with dust-to-gas mass ratios reaching approximately $10^{-3}$ for the $0.5$ C/O scenario and $10^{-4}$ for the $0.02$ C/O scenario. Furthermore, the presence of dust facilitates more effective energy transport, resulting in a smaller remnant core and a reduced likelihood of core collapse for the $1 M_{\odot}$ models, which can evolve into white dwarfs or neutron stars. This paper introduces Far3Det, a new benchmark designed to evaluate the challenges of 3D object detection and localization in distant scenarios. Existing works often struggle in these environments, yielding poor performance due to adverse factors such as rain, snow, and fog, which degrade sensor capabilities. While current research has examined weather impacts on 2D detection and generated synthetic datasets to simulate them, these approaches fail to address the complexities of real-world 3L detection and localization in inclement conditions. Consequently, Far3Ext collects extensive, real-world, outdoor 3L data across various weather conditions to fill this gap. The framework categorizes these conditions into two primary groups: atmospheric scattering and non-atmospheric scattering. The study focuses on quantifying the effects of these atmospheric conditions on detection performance. Analysis reveals that the performance decline caused by atmospheric scattering is significantly more severe than that of non-at atmospheric conditions. Furthermore, the paper explores the influence of distance on detection accuracy under such conditions, finding that performance deteriorates more rapidly with distance in non-atmospheric scattering environments compared to uniform or linear patterns. Finally, the authors introduce a new metric, the Far3D Score, to measure and evaluate a sensor's ability to detect and localize objects at a distance.

Finding the ground state of quantum many-body systems is a significant challenge, particularly for those too large for traditional computational methods. To address this, we propose a novel strategy that combines neural networks with a Lanczos algorithm to generate approximate ground states. In our approach, a single Lanczos vector is mapped by a neural network onto a state within the target system's Hilbert space; the network parameters are then optimized using the Lanczos algorithm's criterion to minimize the energy. Results indicate that our method achieves high accuracy, successfully determining ground state energies and computing spin correlation functions. Furthermore, the model demonstrates the ability to identify ground state degeneracy and detect topological phase transitions by analyzing long-range spin correlations.

The energy-momentum tensor for a spacetime exhibits complete conformal invariance under any spacetime that admits a conformal mapping to a Scharnschild spacetime. By utilizing the components of this energy-momentum tensor, we have derived the specific conformal vector for spacetimes exhibiting spherical symmetry and stationarity. It is important to note that the spacetime associated with this energy-momentum tensor allows for an Killing vector corresponding to the conformal vector under these conditions. We compare our derived results against prior work concerning the Cardy-Cardy vector in a black hole context, finding that they align perfectly. Consequently, the results support the application of a Cardy-Cardy formulation to compute the Cardy-Cardy entropy within the context of gravitational anomalies.

Unsupervised scene flow estimation (SFE) predicts the three-dimensional motion field and relative camera displacement from a pair of consecutive frames. Due to the inherent ambiguity of such stereo motions, learning robust models requires adversarial metric training. However, this approach depends on precise depth estimations, which are often compromised by intentional or incidental adversarities. Specifically, models trained using standard datasets suffer from issues like motion blur, illumination changes, and noise, leading to significant estimation errors. Furthermore, models trained in real-world settings face additional challenges from various sources of adversity, including those that are intentional and noise. Consequently, the accuracy of neighboring frames is often unreliable, undermining the effectiveness of the training process. This paper introduces a new methodology for estimating scene flow and metrics independently, without relying on neighboring frames. The proposed approach involves retraining the model using an updated loss function designed to address these specific adversarial conditions, thereby improving the accuracy of flow and metric predictions in isolation.

Random Neural Networks (RNNs) are a binary-output classifier that categorizes input patterns into "high" or "low" based on whether the membrane potential of a single output neuron exceeds a threshold. This study presents an RNN designed to classify inputs into three groups by duplicating the neuron and incorporating distinct synaptic connection weights. The proposed RNN exhibits sparse activity, enabling energy-efficient operation on neuromorphic hardware, and utilizes stochastic connectivity and weights for simplified biological emulation. While the original publication appeared in *Neural Networks* (Elsevier) in 2019, this version revisits the model's fundamentals, refines the presentation based on reader feedback, and expands the analysis regarding the impact of network parameters on performance. The core classification mechanism relies on the balance between excitatory and inhibitory weights; specifically, the stochastic configuration of these weights determines the ratio of high-inhibition to low-inhibition states, which in turn sets the probability of the output neuron reaching the firing threshold. Empirical results indicate that stochastic weights reliably produce sparse activation patterns, allowing the system to achieve 100% classification accuracy across various input dimensions and levels of noise.

In the high-temperature, high-density environment of a star composed largely of spin-aligned strange quarks, we have investigated how varying magnetic field strengths influence the equation of state (EOS) and the resulting hydrostatic equilibrium. By employing the Nambu-Jona-Shinion model within a grand canonical framework, we determined the thermodynamic properties of these stars across different temperatures and magnetic field intensities. Our EOS calculations were subsequently utilized within the Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkov (TOV) framework to derive the corresponding mass and radius profiles. Results indicate that both the thermodynamic attributes and the structural characteristics of spin-aligned strange quark stars are markedly sensitive to fluctuations in the external magnetic field and internal temperature.

This work introduces an ideal pairing to create a category where objects are simple, connected cubic graphs, while ideal pairings of these graphs serve as the morphisms. We demonstrate that ideal pairings preserve both the number of vertices and edges, as well as a specific edge coloring property we define. Furthermore, we establish a connection between ideal pairings and Hamiltonian circuits within cubic graphs. Finally, we introduce the concept of "HT-tying" edges in such graphs and prove the existence of an "HT-tied" factor graph for every object falling in this categorical framework.

We introduce Timeloops, a static analysis framework designed to automatically generate system call rules for containerized microservices. These rules are essential for generating precise allowed system call whitelists, thereby enhancing the security of microservice deployments. Timeloops generates rules by identifying the specific execution paths taken by a microservice during its initial start-up, utilizing the rule format defined in the generative tool for ReSol. To demonstrate the effectiveness of Timeloops, we conducted an evaluation across eight popular microservices. The results show that the approach successfully produces robust rules that significantly improve the accuracy of system call sandboxing for these services.

Addressing the hierarchy problem and generating dark matter (DM) within a $B-L$ augmented Standard Model is possible via pseudo-Goldstone dark matter (pGDM), where the pGDM mass scale is tied to the symmetry breaking scale. This work extends the analysis to the case of a pGDM that acquires its mass through interactions with the DM sector, specifically within the $B-L$ Standard Model. We establish the necessary conditions for this model to simultaneously account for both dark matter and neutrino oscillation observations. Our findings indicate that this framework can also produce the baryon asymmetry of the universe through the mechanism of out-of-equilibrium pseudo-CP-violating (OEC-PV) processes.

Correspondingly, a generalized Probability Hypothesis Density (PHD) and Generalized Multi-Bernoulli (GBB) consistent Joint Probabilistic Data Association (JPDA) measurement generation density are defined to facilitate the derivation of consistent Posterior Marginal Birth (PMB) filters. These components collectively form the GPGP filter framework. This study investigates the null controllability within a species dynamics model featuring a degenerate diffusion operator defined on a bounded domain. Specifically, the degradation occurs along a specific sub-region where the diffusion coefficient becomes zero, and the study examines various boundary conditions. The article establishes sufficient conditions for controllability when the boundary is non-homogeneous and determines the minimal possible time required to achieve a homogeneous state. Furthermore, full controllability proofs are provided for both Dirichlet and Neumann configurations, utilizing a cost function that grows exponentially with time. Finally, the paper addresses a scenario in which a sub-domain acts as a heat source, demonstrating that heat supply from this source facilitates the system's null controllability.

Soccer represents a dynamic sport characterized by continuous evolution, where tactical decisions are pivotal to a team's success. To improve performance during critical match moments, this study applies Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) to optimize team strategies. We introduce a novel Markov Decision Process (MDP) formulation tailored to soccer, incorporating four distinct states and three possible actions. A Multi-Agent Deep Q-Network (MAP-DDQN) algorithm was employed to train virtual soccer agents, with performance validated through extensive simulations. The results indicate that our proposed strategy significantly improves team performance compared to baseline approaches.

Expanded source inversion (ESI) serves as an effective strategy for simultaneously refining the velocity and reduced scalar density density potentials within the linearized wavefield equations. Traditionally confined to the frequency domain, this approach has not effectively addressed the complexities of time-domain acoustic wave equations. This study introduces an innovative time-domain expanded source waveform inversion (TD-ESI) framework. The core of this method involves iteratively updating the source term in the time-domain wave equation, with the residual between the simulated and observed data serving as this source term adjustment. To guarantee the stable convergence of the system, the source term updates incorporate a smoothing operator derived from the Hermitian form of the time-domain wave equation. The core linearized time-domain wave equation is solved iteratively using a quasi-Newton approach, where the source term update is defined by the residual error and the inverse of the source term's Jacobian matrix. This Jacobian matrix is approximated by the Hermitian form, which is itself adjusted dynamically through the current state of the density and velocity fields. The efficacy of this proposed TD-ESI method is validated using both synthetic experiments and real-world field data.

In this study, we present an experimental demonstration where quantum compression is employed to generate optical asymmetry within a symmetric nonlinear system. Specifically, by injecting a squeezed vacuum state into one port of a $\chi^{(3)}$ nonlinear medium, we successfully broke time-reversal symmetry in the system's linearized dynamics, even when the intrinsic linear coefficients preserved time-reversal symmetry. This breakthrough allowed us to generate two optical asymmetric states, distinguished by their distinct levels of isolation, utilizing varying levels of input compression. Furthermore, we observed that both states exhibit quantum correlations between their quadratures, which can be harnessed to create a continuous-variable quantum encryption key.

This study examines the X-ray properties of the X-ray pulsar IGR J19294+1816 during its 2019 eruption, utilizing data from the AstroSat observatory. The spectral characteristics were analyzed through the lens of the accretion disk model by Chakrabarti & Mitra (1996), while the spin period and spectral timing variations were investigated using Power Density Spectra (PDS). Our spectral analysis reveals that the source's X-ray emission spans a broad range, with the power law index ($\Gamma$) fluctuating between 2.1 and 3.1 throughout the observation. The model-derived X-ray luminosity reached approximately $1.1 \times 10^{37}$ erg s$^{-1}$, representing roughly 5% of the non-rotating neutron star's Eddington limit. Furthermore, spectral fitting indicates a hydrogen column density of $N_H = (1.0 \pm 0.1) \times 10^{20}$ cm$^{-2}$ and a magnetic field strength at the stellar surface of $B = (1.0 \pm 0.1) \times 10^{13}$ G.
